title: My thoughts on Melancholia; Its excellent, authentic portrayal of depression and my disagreements with the worldview presented in the film by Von Trier.

commenti.body:
Wow, what an excellent article. I have nothing add but I do have a question though?

> My understanding of Lars Von Trier is that he views depression as a rational response to the evil of existence, a sentiment that Justine herself echoes in the film (“I know we’re alone. Life on earth is evil. Life is only on earth. And not for long.”). It’s not uncommon to see these sorts of beliefs among people with depression: that they see the world for what it is and understand the cruelty of life itself, that they can handle catastrophe/crisis better than average folk because of what the illness puts them through.

Do you have any quotes from Von Trier where he actually expresses this belief?

Oh sure! He addresses [it directly here.](https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/lars-von-trier-film-inspired-by-depressive-episode/)

> During a conversation with Female, von Trier said: “My analyst told me that melancholiacs will usually be more level-headed than ordinary people in a disastrous situation, partly because they can say: ‘What did I tell you?’. But also because they have nothing to lose. And that was the germ of Melancholia. From then on, things were speeding up. Less than a year later, the script was written, the actors found, and the crew in the process of shooting.”


In the article he also says how sees hinself in Justine and how the film is based on his personal experience with doomsday prophecies and depression. There was also another quote where he talks about how everyone should experience depression once in their lived but for the life of me I can't seem to find it.

Thanks for your article.

For me that film looked like "Nu, Pagadi!" shouted towards those seemingly happy - you will see, when the push comes to shove we, the depressed ones will be on top. Meanwhile we can vail in misery and look awn on those happy go lucky stupid sheeples.

I saw how it unravels on various scale. Several times.

Long stories short- you never know how you will react when the sky starts to fall- stress brings the worst and the best of people. All your theories go down the drain. But there's a danger of thinking that depression is the right way. If my own life and talks with survivors taught me anything- you must cling to something. God, morals, love, adrenaline, will to see another day. IDK if Tier read any accounts of concentration camps or Gulags. There was a running theme in those memories- you might be the strongest and fattest but when you give up you are as good as dead.

Jesus, that's so much next level shit.   
That analysyst seems like he tells him what he wanted to hear.  
  
And that part about nothing to lose- I'd like to sit this man with my grandpa and his brothers- you see, between them they had 10+ years to observe people in extremely stressful situation and had very strong opinion about who was predisposed to threw himself on electric fence.

I wonder if mr Von Tier or his analysyst had really been in really disastrous situation?    
  
On a spectrum- from "I don't know how I afford my next meal" throught "my spouse is dead and I'm left with two toddlers who ask for mom" to "we are evacuating hospital while advancing army is two blocks away and we hear the cries of slaughtered civillians". 

Even if we talk about just depression- they are not equal. Read Carrie Fisher memories for accounts how violent episodes can be. And what about additional stress? When you can't get up but you are the breadwinner? When you run outside and cry to your mother in law that you can't go back because there's that impulse to end things with your baby?   
   
 I feel for his "melancholy"- but ultimately he was able to afford and focus on treatment in comfortable conditions and even find a source of inspiration. 

And for those who had nothing to lose- survivors of concentration camps would have a word with them- about those who one day didn't get up. Or got up and walked straight towards guards.

You are saying that the depressed person does not have a deeper truth of life in sight, yet the movie is hammering you over the head with the fact of inevitable death and the meaninglessness of everything in light of that. Is that not… accurate? That everything will pass? I feel like you never allow the nihilistic position to be fully expressed, which makes it much easier to put it to the side when discussing the adaptive or maladaptive qualities of depression. The movie is not really interested in how a person keeps living well or poorly, it is exploring what everything means at the end of time.
Nihilism is not the same as depression. You can be joyful and still find the world has no meaning, depression isn’t a privileged state of mind that has this exclusive insight.

I don’t know that I implied that it was the same, I’m just stating that talking about the maladaptive or adaptive qualities of depression seems to be missing the point when the world is ending. The crushing imminent reality of THE END OF EVERYTHING is not being given the focus it deserves in this analysis of the film in my opinion.

Yes, exactly. My argument is not against nihilism or anti-natalism. I'm just arguing that depression(a debilitating illness) shouldn't be viewed as an enlightened state of mind that automatically gives you any unique insight into life.

Yes, we are going to die. But how we spend time between now and death matters.   
  
In my opinion that contrived scenario just showscases how shallow and wishful the premise is.   
World is full of catastrophes he could chose from- personal to national, from natural to man made- yet he had to resort to end of the world. 

  
Maybe because subconsiciously he feels how false it is and those with nothing to cling to and nothing to lose are the first to end things or just give up where there is always a glimmer of hope?

About your last point, there is a text which I think really opens up the discussion on futility, depression, nihilism and resistance called [Blessed is the Flame](https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/serafinski-blessed-is-the-flame#toc26). This has a very interesting take on what you said about memories, stress and delusion. In it there is a reference to another important theory of “Cruel Optimism”. 

In her book Cruel Optimism, Lauren Berlant dissects some of the reasons that human beings cling so tenaciously to hopeful ideas. She defines “cruel optimism” as “a relation of attachment to compromised conditions of possibility whose realization is discovered either to be impossible, sheer fantasy, or too possible, and toxic.”

 I always saw Lar’s work to not only play with the idea of depression, but the themes of a cruel nature of reality and the futility of our existence within it. I think themes of depression, nihilism, cruel optimism and bad faith play a major role in most of his work.

> But there's a danger of thinking that depression is the right way. If my own life and talks with survivors taught me anything- you must cling to something. God, morals, love, adrenaline, will to see another day. IDK if Tier read any accounts of concentration camps or Gulags. There was a running theme in those memories- you might be the strongest and fattest but when you give up you are as good as dead.

That's my experience as well. At the end you need some semblance of hope(anything really) to power through dark times.

There is not always a glimmer of hope despite your statement that there is, and this movie is about a situation where there inarguably is no hope, and all you are able to do is dismiss it as contrived and refuse to engage. You are not really engaging with the movie, I would contend.

Things that will happen in couple hundreds of years will be another woman's problem. Wish her the best. Honestly I don't see a connection with natural passage of time and waiting for horrific and painful death of everyone I love.

Agreed. Part of the CBT treatment for depression is specifically helping depressed people see that a lot of their views about the world are based in cognitive distortions, not a more accurate view of the world. Realizing that one’s views are not a more accurate insight into the world can be critical in letting those views ago and working to make your self talk more positive. 

Validating that’s depressing realism is a more accurate view of the world is both incorrect in my opinion, but also damaging to recovery for those who are clinically depressed. It’s also totally understandable that Lars views his outlook that way, it’s a common belief among those with depression.

Safe bet, they don't have the first-hand knowledge of the nuance. But I do hope that the nuance had been laid out and explained to them based on other people's cases, and not on their own experiences.

I've seen so much research go into the tiniest and dumbest details of his films, so especially with Lars Von Trier I think we're in a better camp to presume "quality research" before much else. 

I would imagine they're well aware that they don't have the breadth of trauma-responses in their bodies to envision an entire family's reaction to an apocalypse.

Agreed, but that's a natural result of the conversation around this piece. The hero of this circumstance is the one who's already sad enough to endure it, like the rest of life. That's a pretty controversial point to make your audience walk away with, for sure. 

As a person in a family with two manic depressives, I'm not mad about this despite it saying something that upsets people. Those family members come into my life sometimes and act like heros in the weirdest and most non-conformative ways, and a lot of it is due to their mindset being extremely refreshing to mine.

If you can’t see how a movie about the end of the world brings to mind questions of human meaning in the face of the inevitability of death and the passage of time, I’m not sure what to say. They seem deeply, inextricably related to me.

I work with dying people. You may make peace with death and time, find your own meaning or just have it very deeply... somewhere.  The prospects of catastrophe cutting brutally you and your loved ones life short are completely diffrent thing.

I really have hard time imagining self-respecting psychologist telling patient that they are superheroes because they have nothing to lose. "Depressive realism" is at best very flaved theory so making it a base of whole premise implies a lot of omission.

That’s fair and certainly true. I think that the movie has less of a moralizing stance than OP does, and I don’t know that I ever took from it the idea that Justine’s worldview is good or the correct one, but I certainly could find things to understand and resonate with and I found the movie very compelling and thought provoking. It is a work of art wallowing in despair and hopelessness, which I respect and think has a place but I can certainly understand finding it miserable or even unhealthy. Also, unrelated but thank you for doing that kind of work, you clearly have a very empathetic and kind heart.

Megalopolis is built on the fact that "Hope for Utopia is just irresponsible escapism." That's... uh.... based on a fraction of history and extremely unhelpful to those aspiring to make their worlds better.

It's not a good point to make. But it has merit and real world value. And creates conversation where there was once not enough. 

I don't think it's so simple as any single statement to walk away with. The point isn't "depression is a superpower." But asking "why did the director feel it was important to show the downtrodden as the heroes" is right. And in a way, I theorize it was a patch to put on a society which finds mental health conversation beneath them. 

That perspective is not very American at all, so if we're chatting from the US, I don't think this theme and time are one that we can dissect without the context of the creator.

Depression is an inward ailment, it's about your place in the world and purpose. External circumstances can affect it, sure, but to compare external circumstances tells me you don't understand what depression is at the core.

I don't take the film as proposing that it is right to be depressed, rather it is proposing a specific, fantastic scenario, in which it is.

It's similar to how Hereditary plays with mental illness but then "justifies it" by tying it to actually supernatural events.

It'a about chemicals in your brain.   
You can put any other disease- you can be sick in luxury facility or chosing between medicine and food for children and I find it rich when former tells the latter that it's a blessing.

Thanks.   
I don't think I'm particulary empathetic or kind, just found my a niche where I can put my talents to use. I'd lie if I tell that I didn't chose it partially because I wante to see some kind of meaning in my life and I wasn't cut to be nun, activist or teacher.

tristan and isolde is an interesting choice because it ends with the peaceful acceptance of death with liebestod

https://youtu.be/OAEkTK6aKUM?si=evnOF6kZ1-MFQ8A2

"Shall I drink,
immerse?
Sweetly in fragrances
melt away?
In the billowing torrent,
in the resonating sound,
in the wafting Universe of the World-Breath ---
drown

be engulfed ---
unconscious ---

supreme bliss"

> It'a about chemicals in your brain.

It's not that simple.

Have you experienced depression?

It really has nothing to do with external circumstances. Suicide rates are higher among people with higher income and higher quality of life.

> and I find it rich when former tells the latter that it's a blessing.

That's a judgement that you're making personally but it has nothing to do with what is depression.
Not sure why you are getting downvoted…

I think you've fundamentally misunderstood what von Trier is saying here and are connecting it to a philosophical point he's not really making. he's not suggesting that depressed people have greater insight or a more enlightened view on the reality of the world, but simply that they react less when real catastrophe does happen (and not that they have greater predictive capacities or a better understanding of how those catastrophes happen). speaking from personal experience, serious depression and general pessimism does level your sense of emotional reactivity, since you're obviously more willing to accept bad outcomes if that's basically what you already expect.

 that's especially relevant in the film because everyone is faced with the same impending catastrophe; Justine doesn't have better insight than anyone else into whether or not the planet is actually going to be destroyed, she's just more resigned to that eventuality because it fits with her preexisting sense of pessimistic fatalism. she already believes that life is evil and futile, so she's not bothered by the end of the world, but that doesn't mean she's right in believing that.

Nice. The inversion of power in the late stages of the film, where Dunst flourishes in the face of doom while Gainsbourg wilts, always seemed full of shit to me. Believe me, having severe depression doesn't make you fare any better in a crisis. As you rightly say, the evidence for depressive realism is mixed, at best; like most of the research in social psychology that has broken through to the general public, it's failed to replicate.

Even more bollocks is the fate of Sutherland's sunny rationalism, which is just pure schematism on the part of von Trier, much like what Skarsgard does  at the end of Nymphomania -- it doesn't flow from the characters; it's just von Trier arranging the characters to make a philosophical point about Men and Reason and all that.

On the other hand, there's that scene the morning after the wedding when her new husband leaves. I can't remember the exact detail, but amid the flaming wreckage she has made of their new marriage, Dunst says something like "well, what did you think was going to happen?" and he just nods with resignation like, yeah, okay fair enough. I think about that scene *all the time*
